section.title: Freedom in Christ
section.sectionRationale: The doctrinal argument becomes a ringing call to action. It is for freedom that Christ has set us free, so the Galatians must stand firm and not take on the yoke of slavery. To be circumcised to be justified is to be severed from Christ and fallen from grace; what counts is faith working through love. Freedom is not license but the freedom to serve one another in love, fulfilling the law in a single command.
section.thesis: Christ has set us free for freedom, so believers must stand firm and refuse the yoke of the law, for seeking justification by law severs one from Christ and falls from grace; true freedom is not a license for the flesh but faith working through love, serving one another and fulfilling the whole law in the command to love your neighbor.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to stand firm in freedom and the warning that circumcision for justification severs from Christ; faith working through love as what truly counts, and the warning against the agitators; and freedom rightly used, serving one another in love and fulfilling the law.

units.label: Stand firm in freedom
units.note: do not take on the yoke of slavery

verses.text: It is for {{eleutheria|freedom}} that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.
Take notice: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all.
Again I testify to every man who gets himself circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law.
You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from {{charis|grace}}.

units.label: Faith working through love
units.note: what truly counts, and a warning to the agitators

verses.text: But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness.
For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. What matters is faith expressing itself through {{agape|love}}.
You were running so well. Who has obstructed you from obeying the truth?
Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you.
A little {{zume|leaven}} works through the whole batch of dough.
I am confident in the Lord that you will take no other view. The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.
Now, brothers, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been abolished.
As for those who are agitating you, I wish they would proceed to emasculate themselves!

units.label: Freedom to serve in love
units.note: the whole law fulfilled in one command

verses.text: For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love.
The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another.

eleutheria.gloss: Freedom, liberty. This is the banner of the whole letter: Christ has set us free, and the purpose of that freedom is freedom itself, life released from the law as a means of acceptance and from bondage to sin. Yet Paul is careful, freedom is not license; it is liberty to love and serve. To go back under the law is to trade this freedom for a yoke of slavery.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unearned favor. To try to be justified by the law is to fall away from grace, verse 4, abandoning the only ground on which anyone stands before God. Grace and law keeping as a way of salvation cannot be mixed; to choose one is to lose the other. The believer lives entirely within the sphere of grace.

agape.gloss: Love, self giving love that seeks the good of the other. Faith is not idle; it expresses itself through love, verse 6. And freedom is exercised precisely in serving one another in love, so that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbor. Love is the shape true faith takes and the way freedom is rightly used.

zume.gloss: Leaven, yeast, a small agent that spreads through the whole lump of dough. Paul warns that the false teaching, though it may seem a small matter like circumcision, will work through the entire community and corrupt it. A little error about the gospel does not stay small; it permeates and ruins, which is why it must not be tolerated.

basic.context: Paul turns from argument to appeal. Christ has set the Galatians free, so they must stand firm and not put on the yoke of the law. If they get circumcised in order to be justified, they cut themselves off from Christ, because they are trusting law rather than grace. What counts is faith that works through love. Freedom is not a license to sin but the freedom to serve one another in love.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the pivot of the letter, from doctrine to life. The freedom Paul defended is now the freedom he commands them to protect and to use rightly. Read the stern warnings and the call to love together: the same gospel that frees from law frees for love.
basic.originalLanguages: The keyword is eleutheria, freedom, the freedom Christ won. To seek justification by law is to fall from charis, grace. What counts is faith working through agape, love. And the false teaching is like zume, leaven, a little of it spreading through the whole church.
basic.typology: The yoke of slavery recalls the bondage of Egypt, from which God freed His people to serve Him. Christ is the greater exodus, setting us free not to do as we please but to love. Loving your neighbor as the fulfillment of the law points to Christ, who fulfilled it perfectly in laying down His life.
basic.christ: Christ set us free, and to add law to Him is to lose Him: Christ will be of no value to those who seek justification by circumcision. The offense of the cross, that we are saved by Christ crucified alone and not by our works, is the very thing the agitators want to remove. Christ crucified is the ground of both our freedom and our love.
basic.god: God is the One who calls the Galatians, and the false persuasion does not come from Him. He is the God of grace from which they must not fall. The Spirit He gives is the power by which believers await the hope of righteousness and serve in love. God frees His people to love as He has loved them.
basic.crossReferences: John 8 says the Son sets us free and we are free indeed. Romans 13 says love is the fulfilling of the law. 1 Corinthians 5 uses the same image of a little leaven spreading through the lump.
basic.oneStory: God is a liberator. As He freed Israel from Egypt to worship Him, so Christ frees His people from sin and law to love. The story runs from bondage to freedom, and the freedom is completed not in self indulgence but in a community that serves one another in love, fulfilling the law God always intended.

context.literary:
Galatians 5:1 is the hinge on which the letter turns, and it is built to be read both ways. Looking back, it summarises the long argument of chapters 3 and 4: Christ has done the freeing. Looking forward, it launches the commands of chapters 5 and 6, beginning with 'Stand firm.' A good deal of the force of the section comes from this double motion, an indicative followed at once by an imperative.

Verses 2 to 12 are a sustained piece of confrontation. Paul's style grows sharp and personal. 'Take notice: I, Paul, tell you' in verse 2 is an apostolic formula, and the quick stream of warnings that follows, 'obligated to obey the whole law,' 'severed from Christ,' 'fallen away from grace,' comes in three short blows. Then, in verses 5 and 6, he steps out of the warning mode into the positive statement of what faith, Spirit, hope and love actually look like. The contrast between the two halves is deliberate: law-keeping ends in being cut off, while faith ends in a hope that waits eagerly.

Verses 7 to 12 fall into a second pattern of question and answer. 'You were running so well' is an athletic image that Paul has used before, Galatians 2:2, and the questions that follow lead to the short proverb in verse 9 and a confident word in verse 10. Verses 11 and 12 are a bitter personal aside, in which Paul turns from the troublers to himself and then back to them.

Verses 13 to 15 move from freedom to the way freedom is used, and so prepare for the whole of the rest of the letter. The pivot word is 'but' in verse 13, followed by the sharp and tender 'serve one another in love.' The pattern of verse 14 is a compact summary of the law, then verse 15 gives the dark picture of what happens when love is absent, a fight between animals. The structure in the end is a ring: freedom, a warning about law, a positive statement about faith and love, a warning about the troublers, and freedom again, this time with love as its shape.
context.historical:
Circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham, Genesis 17:10-11, and for Jews of Paul's day it was the clearest line between those inside and those outside the people of God. Gentile men who wished to join Israel had long been expected to receive it. The agitators in Galatia were therefore making an argument that sounded loyal to Scripture: if you want to be in Abraham's family, take the sign God gave Abraham. It was probably also an easier path socially. Jews were allowed to practise their religion in the empire, and Gentile Christians who were not circumcised could appear to be members of a new and unrecognised group.

Paul's remark about being persecuted in verse 11 shows the cost. He suggests that his enemies might claim he still preached circumcision, perhaps because he had circumcised Timothy, Acts 16:3, or because of what he had done before his conversion. His reply is that if he were, the persecution would have stopped. In Galatians 6:12 he says plainly that those who press circumcision want to avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ.

Verse 12 would have struck the Galatians with unusual force. The region of Galatia was associated with the worship of the mother goddess Cybele, whose priests were known for castrating themselves, and Paul's wish that his opponents would go all the way carries a bite that depends on that background. Even without it, the verse is a savage joke at the expense of those who value a minor cut so highly.

The picture of 'leaven' in verse 9 would have been vivid in a society of daily baking. Leaven was a bit of fermented dough kept from the last batch, and Israel was told to remove it from the house at Passover, Exodus 12:15. That background made it a natural symbol of something small that spreads and changes everything.
context.canonical:
The language of freedom in verse 1 has deep roots in the exodus. The Lord said, 'I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness,' Leviticus 26:13. Yoke is a standard biblical image for burden and rule, whether of a harsh master, as in Jeremiah 28:13-14, or of the law, as Peter says in Acts 15:10. Jesus offered a different yoke, 'My yoke is easy and My burden is light,' Matthew 11:29-30, and Paul sets his readers between the two.

The warning about being 'obligated to obey the whole law' reaches back to Deuteronomy 27:26, quoted in Galatians 3:10, 'Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.' The Mosaic covenant could not be taken in pieces. Paul uses that wholeness against those who thought they could add one sign and stop. James makes a related point in James 2:10.

The summary of the law in verse 14 is Leviticus 19:18, a verse set in a chapter full of concrete commands for community life. Jesus put the same verse beside the love of God as the second of the two commandments on which the Law and the Prophets hang, Matthew 22:37-40, and Paul repeats it in Romans 13:8-10 and James calls it 'the royal law,' James 2:8.

The remark about leaven turns up again in 1 Corinthians 5:6, where Paul uses the same proverb about a different sin, and in Jesus' warning about the leaven of the Pharisees, Matthew 16:6-12. In both, the point is the same: a small corruption of teaching or conduct spreads. Taken together, the passage pulls on the exodus, the law and the prophets, the teaching of Jesus and the other letters of the New Testament.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant the Galatians to leave this section knowing where to stand and what to do. 'Stand firm' is a military command, and Paul wanted them to hold their ground against a movement that was presenting itself as the more serious form of Christianity. He argues that the more serious path is the one that does not weaken the cross. To add circumcision to faith as a requirement for acceptance is not an additional blessing but a replacement, because it treats the cross as unfinished.

He was equally concerned to protect them from the opposite error. A church that heard only 'you are free' might take freedom as permission. So he did not leave verse 13 to chance. The same breath that tells them they were called to freedom tells them what the freedom is for, and he gives the church a way to test its own life: Are we serving one another, or biting and devouring?

He also meant to restore their confidence in him. The near-sarcastic questions in verses 7 and 11 invite them to compare his teaching with the opposition's, and to notice who is paying a price for what they preach. The goal of the whole section is not to win an argument but to bring back people who had been running well.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Paul's strong language about severing and falling is a warning aimed at a specific danger, those who were considering accepting circumcision as a way to be justified. It is a description of what that choice would mean, and it is meant to prevent it. Readers should be careful about turning the sentence into a general formula for deciding who is saved and who is not.

The curse on the agitators in verse 10 and the remark in verse 12 are Paul's own reactions to those who were harming the Galatians' faith. They describe how seriously he took the matter. They are not a model for how believers speak to opponents today, and Paul himself calls for gentleness in Galatians 6:1. The coarse joke of verse 12 should not be copied as a pattern for Christian speech.

The command to stand firm, to serve in love and to avoid biting and devouring one another is plainly prescriptive for every believer. The summary of the law in verse 14 is also a standing principle: the whole of the law's moral demand to others is gathered in love of neighbour. It does not abolish the particular commandments but shows their purpose, so that love, rather than the cleverness of a legal loophole, shapes the use of freedom.

debates.question: What does it mean to be 'severed from Christ' and 'fallen away from grace'?

views.label: True believers can lose salvation by turning to law
views.case: Taken at face value, the language says that people who were in Christ can be cut off. Those who hold this view point to the strength of the verbs and to the parallel warnings in Hebrews 6:4-6, and they say Paul would not warn against something impossible.

views.label: A warning about a false profession
views.case: Others say Paul describes what the choice would show about the person making it. Those who rely on law for standing show that they have never truly depended on Christ, because one cannot have both as a basis. This view appeals to 1 John 2:19, that those who went out from us were not of us, and to Paul's confidence in verse 10 that the Galatians will take no other view.

views.label: A statement about the two systems, not a verdict on persons
views.case: A third reading sees Paul laying out the logic of the two ways. The aim is to make clear that grace and law-keeping cannot be mixed as the ground of acceptance, whichever way individual cases fall out. The Galatians are warned from the edge of the cliff, not told they have already gone over.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree on what Paul wants: the Galatians must not move to law as the ground of their standing. The warning is real, the cure is staying with Christ alone, and Paul himself writes with hope in verse 10 rather than despair.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by 'if I am still preaching circumcision'?

views.label: A charge that he sometimes taught circumcision
views.case: Paul may be answering a rumour that he was inconsistent, preaching circumcision to some audiences. Timothy's circumcision in Acts 16:3 could have given the rumour a seed. Paul replies that his persecution proves otherwise.

views.label: A reference to his life before conversion
views.case: The word 'still' suggests that once he did preach circumcision, as a Pharisee zealous for the law, and he now says he has stopped. On this reading the sentence is a rhetorical question about a past he has left behind.

views.label: An accusation that his silence on it counted as preaching it
views.case: Some think the opponents argued that Paul secretly approved of circumcision since he allowed Jewish believers to remain circumcised. Paul's answer is that the cross's offense shows his message has not been softened.

debates.bearing: The point stands in every case. Paul treats his own suffering as evidence that he did not preach circumcision as a requirement, because a message that left room for human achievement would not have offended anyone.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul begins with a pair of verbs that are easy to miss in English. In verse 1 he tells them to 'stand firm,' a present imperative that means to keep standing, and to stop being 'encumbered' by a yoke. The second verb is in the passive, so the picture is of a people who allow themselves to be held fast. The yoke of slavery is not imposed on them by force; they are in danger of lifting it onto their own necks.

In verse 4 the Greek for 'severed' is the verb katargeo, used elsewhere by Paul of the law's power being cut away, as in Romans 7:2 and 7:6, where a widow is released from the law of her husband. Here the one cut off is the person trying to be justified by the law, and what is severed is the connection with Christ. The verb 'fallen away' is the word that is used of a flower dropping or a ship being driven from its course. It is in the aorist, which suggests the decisive moment of the change. The tense of 'trying to be justified' is present, a continuing project, and it is the project, not a single act, that Paul says puts a person outside grace.

Verse 6 gives the most important phrase of the chapter: 'faith expressing itself through love.' The participle is in the middle or passive voice and means working or being made effective. Faith is not a bare opinion but a living force that comes to work through love. Paul does not set faith against works in general. He sets faith against law-keeping as the ground of acceptance, and he insists that faith's own energy is love. Compare 1 Thessalonians 1:3, where he speaks of the 'work of faith' and the 'labor of love.'

In verse 13 the word translated 'opportunity' was a military term for a base of operations from which an army launches its campaign. Freedom can become a base for the flesh. The flesh, as Paul uses the word here, is not the body but the self turned in on itself, which is why the cure is to serve, from the same family of words as doulos, slave. The believer is freed from slavery in order to become a slave of one another in love, a deliberate paradox.

In verse 14 the verb for 'is fulfilled' is in the perfect tense. The law has been brought to its fullness and stands fulfilled in the single word of love. It does not say that love replaces the law or discards its commands, but that love is the place where the commands come to rest. Verse 15 uses three verbs of animal violence, biting, devouring and consuming, as a deliberate image of a community without love, wild beasts turning on one another.

typology.fulfillment: God freed Israel from Egypt, broke the bars of their yoke, and brought them out to serve Him, Leviticus 26:13. Paul says Christ has done the greater thing, setting people free from sin and the curse of the law, Galatians 3:13, so that they might serve in love. The correspondence is complete except in scale: Israel left Egypt in a single night, but the freedom Christ won reaches every nation. The type falls short because Israel's deliverance did not alter the heart, whereas the Spirit does, Galatians 5:5 and 5:16.

At Passover, Israel was to clear leaven out of their houses, Exodus 12:15, and Paul uses the same image in 1 Corinthians 5:7-8, where Christ is the Passover lamb and believers are to be an unleavened batch. In Galatians the leaven is the false teaching, and the lesson is that the new community of those who have been redeemed must keep the gospel pure. The type finds its fulfillment in Christ, whose death is the true Passover, and it falls short in that leaven in the Old Testament was a ritual matter, while here it names a doctrinal and moral one.

typology.type: Circumcision and the circumcision of the heart
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament already called Israel to circumcise their hearts, Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6. Paul says in Philippians 3:3 that those who worship by the Spirit of God are the true circumcision. In Galatians 5:6 neither the cut nor its absence has any value, because the sign points to something that only the Spirit can do. The type is fulfilled in Christ's cutting off on the cross and in the new birth. It falls short in that the physical sign marked only males and could be received without a changed heart.

typology.type: Love of neighbour as the fulfillment of the law
typology.fulfillment: The command of Leviticus 19:18 stood in the middle of a code of concrete duties. Jesus gave it as the second great commandment, and Paul calls it the fulfillment of the whole law. In Christ the correspondence deepens, since He loved to the end and gave Himself up for us, John 13:1 and Galatians 2:20, and set a new standard, 'as I have loved you,' John 13:34. The type falls short because the old command measured love by love of oneself, while Christ's love is the new measure.

study.christ:
The whole section circles one person. Paul says in verse 2 that the Galatians stand to lose Christ, and in verse 4 that they will be severed from Him. Those are warnings of a loss of the one thing that matters most. Everything else in the passage is arranged around this: law-keeping as a ground of standing and Christ as a ground of standing cannot be held together, because one assumes the work is still to be done, and the other says it is finished.

The cross is the centre of the argument. In verse 11 Paul says that the offense of the cross would be abolished if he preached circumcision. The cross offends because it says that we cannot save ourselves, that Christ crucified is the only way, and that all human credentials are worthless, 1 Corinthians 1:23. The agitators wanted to preach a Christ without that offense, a Christ who needed a little help. Paul's whole argument is that such a Christ would not be Christ at all.

Freedom itself is Christ's gift and achievement. 'It is for freedom that Christ has set us free,' and Paul has said how, that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The freedom of chapter 5 is therefore not an abstract liberty but the result of a particular death. It is also Christ who supplies the pattern of its use. The one who has all rights took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:5-8, and in washing His disciples' feet He showed what it means to serve one another in love, John 13:14-15. When Paul tells the Galatians to serve one another, he calls them to follow Christ's own way.

The hope of verse 5, 'the hope of righteousness,' also looks to Christ. Believers eagerly await a righteousness that is already theirs by faith, Romans 3:22, and will be fully displayed when Christ appears. They wait through the Spirit, who is the Spirit of Christ, Galatians 4:6.

A caution is needed. Paul does not say that the Old Testament command of circumcision was foolish or that Christ's followers should despise their Jewish heritage. His complaint is about using any sign as a ground of acceptance, and about the new situation after the cross. The sign was a promise pointing to Christ, and once the substance has come, to return to the sign as though it could save is to reverse the order God set.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the One who calls. Paul says in verse 8 that the persuasion pulling the Galatians away 'does not come from the One who calls you.' That description of God as caller is a quiet anchor. The Galatians were not chosen because they kept the law, and they cannot be unchosen by failing to. The call came from God's own initiative, Galatians 1:6 and 1:15, and the false teaching is contrasted with it as something foreign to His voice.

God is the God of grace, and the phrase 'fallen away from grace' shows the nature of that grace as a gift that cannot be mixed with merit. If grace is partly earned it is no longer grace, Romans 11:6. This is the character of the Giver. He does not give with one hand and demand repayment with the other. The passage invites worshippers to marvel at a generosity that cannot be improved upon by human work.

He is the God who judges those who trouble His people. Verse 10 says that the one troubling the Galatians 'will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.' God is not careless about false teaching. The judgment is certain, though Paul does not name it or dictate how it will fall. Those who mislead the vulnerable answer to Him, and His people can rest in that.

He is also the God who gives the Spirit, and who is at work in the faith of those who wait. 'By faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness,' verse 5, is a statement in which Father, Son and Spirit have their own part: the Father who will declare righteous, the Son in whom faith rests, and the Spirit who sustains the waiting. The doctrine of God here is Trinitarian in action even though it is not stated as a doctrine.

He is a God of love, and verse 14 reveals the heart of His law. The whole demand He makes on how we treat each other is gathered into love of the neighbour, and since Paul says in 5:22 that love is the fruit of His Spirit, God not only commands it but supplies it. For worship, the passage teaches that we are not free to do as we like but free to be what God made us to be, a people who serve one another because we have been served by Christ.

crossReferences.note: The source of verse 14. The command to love one's neighbour as oneself stands next to the ban on hatred, revenge and grudges, so it comes with concrete shape. Paul's use shows that the 'single decree' was always at the heart of the law's social teaching.

God says He broke the bars of Israel's yoke and let them walk upright. This is the backdrop to Paul's yoke of slavery, and shows that freedom from a yoke was always something God did for His people before He asked anything of them.

The curse on anyone who does not continue to do all that is written in the law. Paul has already quoted it in Galatians 3:10, and it stands behind his warning in verse 3 that anyone who takes up circumcision as a requirement owes the whole law.

Paul's parallel summary. The commandments about adultery, murder, theft and coveting are 'summed up' in love of neighbour, and love does no wrong to a neighbour. It makes clear that love is not a vague feeling but the practical fulfilling of the law's moral demand.

Jesus joins love of God and love of neighbour as the two commandments on which the Law and the Prophets hang. Paul's single decree in Galatians 5:14 is the second of these, and he is following his Lord in treating it as the key to the rest.

The same proverb about leaven used for a different problem. A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough, so the church is to clear out the old, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. It shows that Paul thought of leaven as a lasting image of how corruption spreads.

The Jerusalem council met over the same dispute. Some taught that unless Gentiles were circumcised they could not be saved, and Peter answered that the law was a yoke neither they nor their fathers could bear, and that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.

Paul warns against those who mutilate the flesh and says believers are the true circumcision, who worship by the Spirit and put no confidence in the flesh. He counts his own credentials as loss for the sake of Christ, which is the same gospel he is defending here.

Paul faces the objection that freedom invites sin. 'Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not!' This parallels the warning of Galatians 5:13 that freedom must not be used as an opportunity for the flesh.

Jesus says the truth will set free those who continue in His word, and that anyone who sins is a slave to sin. 'If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.' The freedom Paul defends is the freedom the Son gives, not a freedom invented by the church.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world made for loving service and sees it unravel through grasping self-rule. The first humans were given a garden and a single limit, and they heard in that limit a threat to their freedom. From then on, the human tendency has been to treat freedom as the absence of any claim on us, and the result has been bondage: to sin, to the powers, to each other. Galatians 5 comes at the question from the other side. Real freedom is not release from every claim but release from the wrong master so that we can be given to the right one.

The exodus is the first great picture. God brought Israel out of Egypt so that they might serve Him, and the book of Exodus keeps joining the two ideas, release and worship, Exodus 7:16. Israel's history after that shows how difficult it is to remain free. They were repeatedly drawn back into the systems of the nations around them, and the law, given as a gift, was turned into a burden and a boundary. The prophets promised something deeper, a new covenant in which God would write His law on their hearts and put His Spirit within them, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27.

Christ is the fulfillment of that promise. His death breaks the curse of the law and opens the way for the Spirit to be given, so that what the law demanded can be carried out in a people who now love. That is why Paul in verse 6 puts faith and love together, and in verses 13 and 14 makes love the shape of freedom. The new covenant community is the place where the law is fulfilled, not by rule keeping alone but by the Spirit's work.

The story ends with a people who are fully free and fully loving. In the new creation there will be no more curse, no more division, and none of the biting and devouring that Paul fears in verse 15. 'The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay,' Romans 8:21, and the children of God will enjoy the glorious freedom that is already their inheritance. The freedom Christ has won will be seen at last as the freedom to love without end.

sermon.title: The Only Thing That Counts (Galatians 5:1 to 12)
sermon.why: Begg calls believers to stand firm in the freedom Christ won, warns that seeking justification by law severs one from Christ, and shows that what truly counts is faith expressing itself through love.

quiz.q: For what purpose has Christ set us free?

options.text: For freedom, so we should stand firm and not take on a yoke of slavery.
options.note: Verse 1 states the purpose and the command together.

options.text: So we can now do whatever we please.
options.note: Freedom is not license for the flesh; it is freedom to love and serve.

options.text: So we can finally earn our salvation.
options.note: The freedom is from earning; salvation is by grace.

options.text: So we can return to the law with new strength.
options.note: Returning to the law is the yoke of slavery Paul warns against.

quiz.q: What happens to those who seek to be justified by the law?

options.text: They are severed from Christ and have fallen from grace.
options.note: Verse 4 states the solemn consequence.

options.text: They become stronger and more mature believers.
options.note: The opposite; they cut themselves off from Christ.

options.text: They gain a second way to be saved.
options.note: There is no second way; law keeping forfeits grace.

options.text: They please God more than others.
options.note: They fall from grace rather than pleasing God.

quiz.q: What does Paul say truly counts in Christ Jesus?

options.text: Faith expressing itself through love.
options.note: Verse 6 makes faith working through love the mark of what matters.

options.text: Whether or not one is circumcised.
options.note: Paul says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value.

options.text: Strict observance of religious days.
options.note: What counts is faith working through love, not observance.

options.text: Public reputation for holiness.
options.note: Reputation is not the point; faith active in love is.

quiz.q: Why does Paul mention a little leaven?

options.text: To warn that a small error about the gospel spreads through the whole church.
options.note: Verse 9 warns of the pervasive corruption of false teaching.

options.text: To praise the growth of the church.
options.note: The image is a warning about corruption, not growth.

options.text: To recommend adding a little law to grace.
options.note: The leaven is the false teaching he opposes, not a recommendation.

options.text: To describe how bread should be baked.
options.note: It is a spiritual warning, not a baking instruction.

quiz.q: How should believers use their freedom?

options.text: To serve one another in love, fulfilling the law.
options.note: Verses 13 and 14 direct freedom toward love.

options.text: As an opportunity to indulge the flesh.
options.note: Paul explicitly forbids using freedom for the flesh.

options.text: To ignore the needs of others.
options.note: Freedom is for serving others, not ignoring them.

options.text: To compete for status in the church.
options.note: That leads to biting and devouring, which Paul warns against.

questions: Christ set you free for freedom. Where are you tempted to put on a yoke of slavery again, whether through legalism or through sin?
Paul says what counts is faith working through love. How is your faith actually expressing itself in love this week?
A little leaven spreads through the whole lump. Where might a small compromise about the gospel be quietly working through your thinking or your community?
Freedom is not license but liberty to serve. Whom is God calling you to serve in love out of the freedom Christ has given?
Paul warns against biting and devouring one another. Where is conflict consuming a relationship, and how might love rather than winning change it?

translationNotes.note: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free renders an emphatic construction; freedom is both the source and the goal of Christ's work, and the verse turns it into a command to stand firm.
The offense of the cross is the stumbling block that salvation comes through Christ crucified alone, not through our works; removing it is exactly what the agitators attempt.
Love your neighbor as yourself quotes Leviticus 19:18; Paul says the whole law is fulfilled in this single command, echoing the teaching of Jesus.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Galatians 5:1-15. Sermon verified this session from the Truth For Life series A Study in Galatians, Volume 1 by Alistair Begg; the movement spans 5:1-15 while the sermon covers 5:1-12.
